specPoints.text: understand that most phenotypic features are the result of polygenic inheritance rather than single genes

primer.text: Single-gene stories are the exception, not the rule. This note names the polygenic pattern — several genes shaping one characteristic — explains why it paints continuous ranges like human height instead of neat either-or classes, and flags why the tidy Punnett square cannot cope, which is exactly what the examiner expects you to know without diagramming it.

lessons.title: Many Genes, Many Phenotypes
lessons.opening: Most of the traits you can see are not single-gene stories at all: several genes interact to build them, which is what polygenic means, and the combined effect is a broad spread of phenotypes rather than a tidy either-or pair.
keyPoints: Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.
Characteristics controlled by more than one gene are called polygenic.
Polygenic traits show a wide range of phenotypes rather than two options.
Height, skin colour and weight are the taught examples.
Simple genetic diagrams struggle to display polygenic inheritance.

low.restatement: Many visible traits come from several genes acting together.
low.analogy: A choir's sound comes from many voices, not one soloist.
low.examPointer: Learn the three examples: height, skin colour, weight.

medium.restatement: Many genes mean many allele combinations, and the combinations map onto a continuous spectrum of phenotypes.
medium.analogy: Mixing paints from many pots yields every shade between the extremes.
medium.examPointer: Say explicitly that you are not expected to diagram polygenic crosses.

check.modelAnswer: Several genes interact to control one characteristic, producing a broad range of phenotypes.

check.stem: List the taught examples of polygenic characteristics.
check.modelAnswer: Height in humans, skin colour and weight.

check.stem: Explain why height in humans forms a continuous spread rather than two classes.
check.modelAnswer: Several height genes each add their own contribution, so the many possible allele combinations blend into a continuous range from short to tall.

check.stem: A student measures the heights of fifty classmates and finds a smooth spread with no two clear groups. What does the pattern suggest about the inheritance of height, and why is a Punnett square the wrong tool here?
check.modelAnswer: The smooth spread suggests polygenic inheritance, and the square is the wrong tool because its four cells cannot represent the many allele combinations several genes produce.

glossary.definition: Controlled by the combined action of more than one gene.
A spread of phenotypes across a spectrum rather than distinct classes.
Controlled by a single gene, the exception for most visible traits.
